title: Minimally Invasive Ross Procedure in Adults, Through an Arrow-Shaped Partial Sternotomy Approach
content: The Ross procedure is highly regarded for its superior long-term outcomes in aortic valve surgery, offering excellent hemodynamic performance and a low risk of valve thrombosis. We present the first 11 cases who underwent arrow-shaped ministernotomy Ross procedure. The surgery began with a 7 cm skin incision, followed by a V”, or arrow-shaped sternotomy to the third intercostal space. The transversal sternal division was made to the superior margin of the fourth rib, in both directions, obtaining an arrowhead shape. Cardiopulmonary bypass was established via central cannulation. The pulmonary autograft was implanted in the aortic position using the miniroot technique, which was followed by the implantation of a pulmonary homograft in the pulmonary position. The cardiopulmonary bypass and aortic crossclamp times were reproducible, with an average of 144 and 86 minutes, respectively. The surgery was completed without complications, and intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography confirmed the successful functioning of the valves. The patients’ postoperative course was straightforward, characterized by a short stay in the intensive care unit and discharge on postoperative day 7-10. Thes cases demonstrate, that the minimally invasive Ross procedure is a safe and effective option in centers with expertise in both minimal access cardiac surgery and the Ross procedure itself. The ministernotomy approach, which provides excellent exposure and reduced surgical trauma, may be particularly beneficial for young, active patients. Given the positive outcomes observed, the approach could be considered a viable alternative to traditional full sternotomy in similar surgical cases.
